analysis: Thomaston has not dated this at all -- the title is pure description, which is itself the tell. A mahogany tilt-top candlestand with a shaped top is the single most reproduced form in American furniture: the Colonial Revival made thousands between 1890 and 1930 that copy the Federal originals closely. The photographs show a snake-foot tripod base and a well-figured shaped top, but nothing in them settles the century.
problems: The whole question is period versus revival, and it is a 130-year spread on the same object. Look underneath at preview: hand-cut irregular saw marks, an off-centre lathe hole, oxidised unfinished surfaces and shrinkage out-of-round all say period. Circular saw marks anywhere say 1830 at the earliest and in practice mean revival. A crisp machine-flat underside is the giveaway.
patience: High. Candlestands run at every Maine sale and a good period one turns up two or three times a year. Do not stretch on an unverified example when the next one is a month away.

analysis: This is the real thing, and the catalogue description now settles what the photographs could not. Thomaston describes an early-20th-century high-shouldered vase in cased green opalescent glass, POSSIBLY BY LOETZ, with Alvin silver overlay in a floral motif, marked at the base edge with the Alvin A and '999/1000 Fine, V10846'. Two things follow. The height is 8 in. -- the open question in the brief, now closed, and it is a desk-scale vase rather than the larger form the seamless-white photograph implied. And the overlay is marked 999/1000, which is fine silver rather than sterling; that is normal for Alvin overlay and it slightly raises the metal quality while leaving the quantity trivial. The Loetz suggestion is the catalogue's own and is worth taking seriously on a cased green opalescent body, though 'possibly' is the house declining to commit.
problems: The height question is closed at 8 in.; what remains is the overlay's condition, which is where silver overlay lots are won and lost -- look for lifting at the edges of the floral work, grey polished-thin patches where a century of cleaning has worn the silver, and hairlines in the glass beneath the metal. 'Possibly by Loetz' is an attribution the house will not stand behind, so do not pay a Loetz premium for it. The silver content is a skin and has no meaningful melt floor whatever the fineness mark says.
patience: Moderate. Alvin overlay appears a few times a year in New England, but examples with this quality of engraved detail and intact silver are less common than the plain scrollwork ones.
sources: Height figures are from the prior session's research, not re-verified here.

analysis: A sterling cigarette case is a melt-plus-a-little object and nothing more. Felmore is a minor American maker, the form is mid-century rather than antique, and the collector market for cigarette cases has been in slow decline for thirty years as the object lost its social context. The only reason to own it is the metal and the fact that a good case is pleasant to handle.
problems: Get the weight. Cases run 3 to 5 troy ounces, so the sterling content is roughly $139 to $231 at the working spot, and a refiner pays 85-90% of that. Deduct any base-metal hinge and the interior gilding, which is not silver. At the $150-250 estimate this is already trading at or above metal, so the estimate is doing the work, not the silver.
patience: Very high. Sterling cases turn up constantly, often in job lots where they cost less than melt.

analysis: The description closes this one. Thomaston names it as 'The Destruction of Tea at Boston Harbor', a HAND COLORED LITHOGRAPH BY NATHANIEL CURRIER for Saxony & Major at 39 Nassau near Fulton Street, New York. That is a specific, checkable printing address, and it is the address Currier worked from in the 1840s -- exactly consistent with the catalogued 1846 date. A named lithographer, a named printer, a named street address and a hand-coloured stone lithograph is not the language used for a 20th-century facsimile. The open question in the brief about whether 1069 and 1070 are originals or later facsimiles is closed in favour of originals. An 1846 N. Currier small folio of the Boston Tea Party at $300-400 is a genuine 180-year-old American historical print inside the band.
problems: Verify the imprint line on the sheet matches the catalogue's Saxony & Major attribution -- that is a two-minute check with the frame in hand and it is the whole basis of the date. Hand colouring fades and the paper will be toned; it is matted under glass so the margins and any foxing are hidden. Small folio is the modest end of the Currier market and the Tea Party is a common subject, so the ceiling is the ceiling.
patience: High for the reproductions, low for genuine large-folio Curriers. Since you cannot yet tell which this is, price it as the common case.

analysis: Also closed by the description, and this is the better of the two. The catalogue gives the full title -- 'Ethan Allen And Mate and Dexter, in Their Wonderful Race Over the Fashion Course, L.I., June 21st, 1867' -- describes it as hand coloured, and supplies the historical context of a $2,000 match race. A large folio Currier & Ives trotting subject with the complete title line is the firm's most commercially successful category, and the specificity of the cataloguing argues for a period impression rather than one of the 20th-century calendar reproductions. $800-1,200 is at the top of the band but a genuine large folio harness racing print supports it.
problems: The catalogue notes one noticeable spot in the sky and minor gilding loss to the frame; a spot in an open sky area is the worst place for it on a print like this and it is a real discount. Large folio is also the size most reproduced, so still put a loupe on the sheet for a dot rosette against continuous stone tone before bidding to the ceiling. Matted under glass, so the margins and the full publication line are hidden.
patience: Moderate. Genuine large-folio trotting prints appear a few times a year, but rarely inside this budget unless condition is poor.

analysis: Watchmaker's tool lots are entirely about what is in the box, and the two photographs here show a general scatter of small hand tools, staking punches and parts tins rather than the one thing that would change the verdict. A Webster-Whitcomb or Boley lathe, or a complete boxed staking set, would justify several hundred on its own. A tray of files, tweezers and loose mainsprings is a $75 lot that three people in the room will bid to $200 because it looks technical.
problems: The catalogue says 'tools and parts', and parts is the word doing the work -- it usually means the residue after the good pieces were sold separately. Count what is actually there at preview and ignore the impression of quantity.
patience: High. Horological tool lots are a Thomaston staple and turn up several times a year.

analysis: Medium resolved, and it changes the picture. The catalogue calls it 'Crashing Whitecaps, OIL ON UPSON BOARD, signed lower right and marked "Maine"'. So it is an oil, not the etching that would have made it cheap -- and Upson board is a pressed wallboard first made in the 1900s-10s, which dates the painting to the second half of Woodbury's career and confirms it cannot be an early work. A signed Woodbury oil of a Maine subject, 19 1/2 x 29 1/2 in., is a $900-2,200 picture. The house's $800-1,200 estimate is if anything light. The open question in the brief is closed: it is an oil, and that puts it out of the band rather than into it.
problems: Above the band once the medium is known -- an oil at this size will not stop at $1,000. The frame is catalogued as damaged gold gesso, which is a cost rather than a bonus. Upson board is dimensionally unstable and warps and delaminates with humidity; check the panel is flat and the paint film is not lifting along the board edges. Note 3467 is a second Woodbury question in this sale, catalogued only 'attributed to' at $300-400 -- that is the cheaper way in, and now the more interesting one.
patience: Moderate for Woodbury generally, high for the etchings specifically -- those come up constantly and cheaply.

analysis: The description closes the weight question exactly and, in doing so, sinks the lot on age. This is a Cooper Brothers & Sons condiment set, Birmingham, 1931, with the two spoons hallmarked Sheffield 1932, and the catalogue states 6.14 ozt tw WITHOUT THE GLASS LINERS -- a stated net weight, which is unusually good practice. That is 191 g of sterling, about $285 of metal and $248 after a refiner. But 1931 is five years the wrong side of the antique line, so the age criterion fails outright on a catalogued date. I had inferred Edwardian-to-George-V from the photographs and put it in the border bucket; the hallmark says otherwise.
problems: Post-1926 by the hallmark, so no age criterion. The metal is real but modest and a $300-500 estimate asks roughly $400-660 all-in against $248 of refiner value -- you are paying for a cased set, not for silver. Cased condiment sets in this pattern are abundant. The cobalt liners are original and intact, which is the one genuinely good thing here, and liners are what these always lose.
patience: Very high. Cased condiment sets are a standing fixture of English silver consignments and frequently fail to sell.

analysis: The photographs confirm the trap exactly as flagged. This is a Washington Mint gilt silver Sacagawea medallion in its original presentation box and capsule -- a private-mint bullion novelty from 2000 with no numismatic standing whatsoever. The gold colour is a plated surface, not gold content, and the word 'golden' in the title is doing dishonest work.
problems: A quarter pound is 113 grams, about 3.6 troy ounces, which is roughly $182 of silver at the working spot and less after a refiner discounts a plated piece. The estimate of $300-500 is nearly triple the metal. When the estimate exceeds melt on a modern bullion item, the estimate is the trap, not the opportunity. The box shows foxing and spotting, which tells you how these were stored and how many survive.
patience: Irrelevant -- these are manufactured in quantity and available online continuously below melt.

analysis: This one is resolved, and the answer overturns the working hypothesis. The margin does not say collotype and 'collograph' is not a typo -- the sheet carries a printed trademark banner reading 'A COLLOGRAPH Print', which is a brand name, and beneath it the line '(c) 1993 Aaron Ashley Inc., Yonkers, N.Y.' with 'Made in U.S.A.' Aaron Ashley is a commercial fine-art reproduction publisher. The title, the artist's name and the 'Collection of Rosalie H. Levine' credit are all printed in the margin as part of the sheet.
problems: There is no pencil signature, no edition number, no publisher of record in the print world's sense, and no date before 1993. This is not the authorised Triton or Aristo collotype and it should not be priced anywhere near one -- the $1,000-2,000 collotype comps are simply the wrong comparison. It is a 1990s photomechanical reproduction of End of Olson's worth $50-100, and in this case the frame and glass may genuinely be worth more than the print inside them.
patience: Irrelevant -- Aaron Ashley Wyeth reproductions are common and cheap.
sources: Read directly off the lot photographs: trademark banner in image 2, copyright line in image 3.

analysis: The house has named the process itself: giclee. That is inkjet on paper, post-1990, with no edition authority behind it and no hand process anywhere in its making. It carries the highest estimate in the entire Wyeth block at $400-600 and has the least substance of anything in it.
problems: Her Room is one of Wyeth's most famous images, which is precisely why it was chosen for reproduction and precisely why the room will bid it. Being the best-known picture in the block and the least authentic object in it is not a coincidence.
patience: Irrelevant.

analysis: Three copies of the Helga portfolio, which was 1987 mass-market art publishing produced in enormous numbers to ride the publicity of the Helga story. Copies trade at $30-100 each and three of them is not a collection, it is a shelf problem.
problems: Quantity is being presented as significance. The $300-400 estimate assumes someone wants three identical portfolios.
patience: Irrelevant -- continuously available.

analysis: One of the seven lots in the block whose catalogue entry says only 'print' with no process named. Given that 1164 has now proved to be a 1993 Aaron Ashley commercial reproduction and 1163 is an admitted giclee, the silence on these should be read as the same class of object rather than as an unstated collotype.
problems: The single most likely explanation for a cataloguer declining to name a process on a famous artist is that naming it would hurt the estimate.
patience: Irrelevant.

analysis: Stow Wengenroth is the finest American black-and-white lithographer of the twentieth century and the one printmaker in this sale whose Maine subjects are genuinely collected outside the state. Nine of his lithographs run consecutively here as lots 1308 to 1316, all estimated $600-800 with $250 openings. Nine at once is a consignment, and consignments of this size routinely exhaust the two or three people in the room who want them -- the last few in a run are where the value is.
problems: Wengenroth editions were typically 250 impressions, so these are not rare, and the estimate band is optimistic for the weaker subjects. Check the margins for a pencil signature -- Wengenroth signed in pencil below the image, and an unsigned trial or a later restrike is worth a fraction. Look also for light-staining and mat burn, which are endemic in mid-century prints that have hung in Maine cottages.
patience: Moderate to high. Wengenroth turns up regularly at Maine sales, but a block of nine lets you be selective on subject and condition rather than taking what appears.

analysis: Maine Coast Seagulls is the most on-brief subject in the Wengenroth run -- explicitly coastal Maine, by the strongest name in the group, and it sits near the end of nine consecutive lots where bidder fatigue does the most work. This is the one to concentrate on if you only want a single Wengenroth.
problems: Being the obvious subject cuts both ways: a title with 'Maine Coast' in it draws the regional bidders who skipped the owl and the sloop. Do not let the subject premium push you past what the print is.
patience: Moderate. The named coastal subjects are the ones that recur least often at this price.

analysis: A framed Maine Steamship Company broadside is exactly the hyper-local material the brief identifies as selling to a small but committed regional audience. Steamship ephemera connects to the Portland-to-New York coastal service and to a specific vanished industry, and framed broadsides display far better than the loose paper they usually survive as.
problems: The catalogue says 'vintage' and 'print', neither of which commits to anything. Broadsides were reprinted for decoration through the 1960s and 70s, and a modern facsimile in an old frame is the common case. Check the paper for period stock and look at the type impression -- letterpress bites into the sheet, offset lithography does not.
patience: Low to moderate. Maine steamship broadsides are genuinely uncommon compared with the general run of nautical prints.

analysis: The albums are described and the answer is good. Thomaston lists a metal cash box of primarily European cards and souvenir sets, PLUS two albums 'both including many Massachusetts, MAINE and New Hampshire views, one with a nice group of REAL PHOTO images', and -- the detail that matters -- one album with twelve cards of the OLD ORCHARD BEACH FIRE OF 1907 published by The Lakeside Press, Portland, and eleven of the San Francisco 1906 earthquake. That is Maine disaster real-photo material from a Portland publisher, which is a specific and collected niche, plus a New England real-photo run. The brief called this the most preview-dependent lot in Day 1; the catalogue has largely answered it, and favourably.
problems: Still a lottery in the sense that nobody has counted the Maine cards or named the towns, and the bulk of the box is European souvenir sets, which are worth very little. The value concentrates in the real-photo album and the Old Orchard Beach group. Postcards in old albums are frequently stuck to the pages or hinged with corners that have bitten into the image; check whether cards can be removed. Open both albums at preview and count the Maine real photos -- that is still the number that decides it.
patience: Moderate. Postcard lots are common but Maine-specific real-photo groupings are what you are actually hunting and those are not.

analysis: Kathodian Bronze Works bookends are not bronze in any useful sense. The company made thin metal shells over composition or plaster cores and finished them to look like cast bronze, and the name was chosen to encourage exactly the confusion the catalogue title now reproduces. Cowboy subjects are common in the line.
problems: The tell is weight and the sound: solid bronze is heavy and rings, a clad shell is light and thuds. Check the underside for the composition core showing through, and for chips at the edges where the shell has separated. Even in perfect condition these are $60-120 objects.
patience: Very high.

analysis: Willard Dryden Paddock was a genuine American sculptor with exhibition history, which puts this in a different category from the Kathodian pair two lots earlier. Signed bookends by a listed sculptor, if actually cast bronze, are a legitimate small-sculpture purchase and the $600-800 estimate is defensible.
problems: Apply the same bronze-versus-spelter test as everything else in this category, and add the foundry question: many sculptors' bookend designs were licensed to commercial founders and later recast. Look for a foundry mark, crisp chasing in the recesses, and a warm patina that varies with wear rather than a uniform sprayed brown.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: A Deco standing female figure initialled CEL is the archetypal spelter-versus-bronze decision, and the archetypal unidentified signature. Per the standing principles, an initial that cannot be resolved to a name is not an attribution and should not be paid for as one. Priced as an anonymous Deco figure, $300-500 is already full.
problems: Spelter is much lighter than bronze, cold to the touch in a different way, and shows grey-white metal wherever the finish has chipped -- check the base edges and the underside. Deco figures are also routinely remounted on replacement marble bases; original bases have consistent wear and matching mounting holes.
patience: Very high. Deco figures of this type run at every general sale.

analysis: Twelve coin silver teaspoons by Palmer, Bacheldres & Co. is the kind of lot that does what the buyer actually wants: genuinely antique, genuinely precious metal, named American maker, and priced as scrap by a room that finds old spoons boring. Coin silver runs about 90% fine, marginally below sterling, and twelve teaspoons is roughly 6 to 8 troy ounces gross.
problems: Weigh them. At 7 ozt of coin silver the metal is about $300 gross and $260 after a refiner, so the $300-500 estimate is at or above melt and the maker premium is what you are buying. Check for monograms -- which the market punishes and you should not care about -- and for bowl-tip wear and repaired handles, which genuinely matter.
patience: High. Coin silver spoons are a constant, though named-maker groups of twelve are less common than mixed lots.

analysis: A dated 19th-century Dutch perfume flask is a clean antique-criterion hit and a pleasant object, but read the words carefully: silver mounted means a collar or cap on a glass body. There is minimal silver content and no melt floor worth calculating.
problems: Dutch silver of this period is often later-marked or has continental duty marks added on import, and small mounts are frequently replaced. Check that the collar fits the glass properly and that the stopper is original -- a married stopper is very common and halves the value.
patience: High.

analysis: Four gold-filled mounted canes. Gold-filled has no melt floor at all -- it is a thin gold layer bonded over base metal, and the word gold in the title should not imply metal value. What you are buying is four decorative sticks.
problems: The $800-1,000 estimate on canes with no precious metal content and no named maker is aggressive. Cane collecting is a real market but it rewards mechanism, gadget and figural carving, none of which is claimed here.
patience: Very high. Cane lots run at most sales.

analysis: An early 19th-century painted box with secret drawers at a $200-300 estimate is one of the better value propositions in Day 1. It is catalogued as early 19th century, so the house has committed; painted surface and interior contrivance are both things the folk-art market pays for; and the estimate is a fraction of what a comparable box makes when it is described as folk art rather than as a box.
problems: Original paint versus later repaint is the whole game. Period paint shows wear where hands went, shrinkage cracks that run through the colour rather than over it, and dirt in the crevices; repaint sits on top and is uniformly bright in the corners. Check the drawers actually work and are original to the box.
patience: Low to moderate. Painted boxes with secret compartments are genuinely uncommon and this is the sort of thing that does not come round often at this money.

analysis: The William Marples Ultimatum brace is the most collected hand tool in the English-speaking world -- brass-framed, ebony-infilled, stamped with the Ultimatum registration, and bought by tool collectors who do not care what else is in the sale. It is a named maker, comfortably antique, and it sits in the budget band.
problems: Ultimatum braces were widely copied and the name was also applied to lesser Marples models. Check the brass plates for the full registered stamp, that the ebony is uncracked at the head, and that the chuck jaws are present and functional. Replaced chucks are common and heavily discount the value.
patience: Moderate. They appear regularly in tool sales but rarely in general antique auctions where the tool crowd may not be watching.

analysis: E.O. Richter of Chemnitz made the best German drafting instruments of the period and a cased Richter set is a properly made object. The value is almost entirely a function of completeness.
problems: Count the instruments against the fitted recesses in the case. Empty slots are money off, and a set missing its large compass or its beam extension is worth a third of a complete one. Also check for corrosion on the German silver and for a case lid that has separated from its hinges.
patience: High. Cased drafting sets are common; complete ones by the top makers less so.

analysis: A Waldoboro fire chief's belt dated c.1890 is hyper-local midcoast material of the sort that sells to a small but committed regional audience and almost never leaves the area. It is catalogued to a date that clears the antique line, it names a specific midcoast town twenty minutes from Thomaston, and firefighting parade regalia has its own collecting base on top of the local one.
problems: Leather of this age is often dry, cracked at the fold, and missing its buckle or lettering. Check that the applied town name and any bullion work are original rather than a later reconstruction, and that the leather will survive being handled.
patience: Low. Named-town Maine fire regalia is genuinely uncommon and this is the honest case for going past comp.

analysis: A hand-made Maine municipal badge is local material with a natural regional buyer, but the catalogue commits to nothing -- no town, no date, no department. Hand-made is doing a lot of work in that title and can mean anything from a period silversmith-made shield to a mid-century replacement.
problems: Establish the municipality and look for a maker's mark on the reverse at preview. An unidentified badge is an anonymous object; a named midcoast town doubles the interest.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: An identified 1863 Maine 6th Volunteer Infantry cartridge box with cap boxes, associated with Gettysburg, is the strongest piece of Maine historical material in Day 1. It is catalogued to a year, tied to a named Maine regiment, and connected to the battle that dominates American Civil War collecting. Identified Maine regimental accoutrements have a dedicated in-state audience quite apart from the national militaria market.
problems: The estimate of $1,000-2,000 is above the budget band and the opening is already $500, so this needs discipline. Identification is everything: ask what the identification actually rests on -- a stamped name, a provenance letter, or an auctioneer's inference. Reproduction Civil War leather is a large industry and the brass plates are cast in quantity. Verify the cartridge box tins are present.
patience: Very low. Identified Maine regimental material with a Gettysburg association is genuinely rare and this is the sort of lot where going to the top of the band is defensible.

analysis: A 19th-century painted shipwright's tool chest is a coastal Maine object in the most literal sense, catalogued to the century, and it hits both the antique and the marine interest at a $400-600 estimate. Shipwrights' chests are larger and better made than domestic tool chests and often retain interior fitted tills and original paint.
problems: Check whether the tools are included -- the title implies the chest alone. Look for original paint versus a decorative repaint, an intact till arrangement, and whether the lid is original. Chests that have been stripped and refinished lose most of their interest.
patience: Moderate. Painted chests are common; documented shipwrights' chests with original surface less so.

analysis: Mark Catesby's Natural History of Carolina plates are genuine 18th-century hand-coloured etchings and among the founding works of American natural history illustration. A real Catesby plate is comfortably antique and a named-maker hit, and $400-600 is a plausible price for a modest subject.
problems: The 1754 and 1771 editions are period; the 1974 Beehive Press facsimiles and various 20th-century reproductions are not, and they are common. Check for a plate mark impressed into the paper, laid paper with visible chain lines, and hand-colouring that sits unevenly on the surface. A sheet with no plate impression is a reproduction regardless of what the frame says.
patience: Moderate. Individual Catesby plates surface regularly but genuine ones inside this budget are usually the less showy subjects.

analysis: Louis John Rhead is a real Art Nouveau name -- an Anglo-American poster designer working in the full Continental idiom in the 1890s, and one of the very few genuine Nouveau practitioners whose work appears in a sale like this. If these are period lithographic posters they are an authentic criterion-three hit; eleven photographs on the lot suggests something substantial.
problems: The $1,000-1,500 estimate is above the budget band and the opening bid is already $500. Rhead's posters have also been reproduced steadily since the 1970s poster revival. Establish whether these are period stone lithographs -- check sheet size against known formats, look for the printer's credit in the margin, and beware of sheets that are too white and too flat.
patience: Low to moderate. Genuine period Nouveau posters are exactly what this buyer says they want and they do not appear often at Thomaston.

date: c.1860-1890 if a period wood engraving
analysis: Winslow Homer at a $1,000-1,500 estimate with fourteen photographs is almost certainly a group or an album of wood engravings from Harper's Weekly rather than anything unique -- and that is not a criticism. Period Harper's engravings are genuinely of the 1860s and 70s, clear the hundred-year line comfortably, and are the only way Homer enters this budget. Homer's Maine connection through Prout's Neck makes them doubly on-brief.
problems: The distinction that matters is a period impression cut from the bound Harper's volume versus a 20th-century restrike or a photographic facsimile. Period sheets show letterpress text on the verso, toned wood-pulp paper and a characteristic slight platemark from the block. Also check whether the estimate reflects a single sheet or the group -- fourteen images suggests several.
patience: High for the engravings themselves, which are common and cheap individually. The reason to look is if this is a substantial group at one money.

analysis: A diminutive oak icebox circa 1900 sits right on the antique line and diminutive is the operative word -- small examples are the ones people actually buy, because a full-size icebox is furniture nobody has room for. Catalogued to c.1900, so the date is the house's claim.
problems: Iceboxes are heavily reproduced as decorative pieces and heavily refinished. Check for original hardware, an intact zinc or galvanised liner, and whether the oak has been stripped. A stripped icebox with replaced hardware is a $150 object.
patience: High. Iceboxes run constantly.

analysis: A 19th-century free-blown glass garden cloche is a satisfying object: catalogued to the century, genuinely hand-made, and the free-blown attribution means seed bubbles, an uneven rim and a pontil scar rather than the moulded reproductions that fill garden centres. At $300-500 it is fairly priced for what it is.
problems: Cloches are fragile and chips at the rim are almost universal -- check how bad. Modern reproductions are common and the tells are a too-even wall thickness, a ground-flat rim and no pontil mark underneath.
patience: Moderate. Genuine period cloches are less common than the market's supply of reproductions suggests.

analysis: A ruby cut-glass double-ended scent bottle, catalogued to the 19th century, is a small, portable, genuinely antique object at $300-500. Double-ended bottles with their original mounts are the collectable version of the form.
problems: The mounts and both caps must be present and original -- a missing or married cap takes most of the value. Check the ruby flashing for wear through to clear glass at the high points, and look for internal residue staining that will not clean.
patience: High. Scent bottles are a standing category.

analysis: John Cary was the leading English commercial mapmaker of the period and three of his European maps at a $300-400 estimate is honest value. Cary maps are properly antique, hand-coloured in outline, and they are the sort of thing that hangs well and holds its modest value indefinitely.
problems: Cary plates were reissued for decades and later impressions from worn plates are weaker. Check for a plate mark, laid paper, and original outline colour rather than modern applied wash. Trimmed margins and backing on board are the common condition problems.
patience: High. Antique maps are a deep and steady market with plenty of supply.

analysis: A circa-1830 handwritten cookbook at $200-300 is one of the quiet good buys in Day 1. Manuscript receipt books are genuinely antique, unique by definition, and increasingly collected as social history rather than as books. If any of the hands can be tied to a New England household the interest rises sharply.
problems: Condition on manuscript volumes is usually poor -- loose boards, foxing, and pages excised. Check how much of it is actually written in; many survive largely blank, which is a different and much cheaper object. Look for an ownership inscription, which is what would let you localise it.
patience: Moderate. Manuscript cookbooks appear a few times a year and are usually cheap because nobody in the room can read them quickly.

analysis: An 1862 Bowdoin College commencement programme is dated Maine ephemera from the middle of the Civil War, which is a genuinely interesting conjunction, and Bowdoin material has a small dedicated collecting base in the state.
problems: Paper ephemera of this kind is fragile and often foxed, folded and edge-torn. The $250-350 estimate is toward the top of what commencement programmes make unless a notable name appears in the class list -- worth reading the names at preview.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: An 18th-century copper bed warmer with a pierced bird decoration is comfortably antique and pleasing, but it sits squarely in the decorative-copper category the brief flags as a weak market. The house has catalogued it to the 18th century, which is the strongest thing about it.
problems: Decorative copper and brass has been soft for two decades and shows no sign of recovering. Handles are almost always replaced -- check whether the turned wood handle matches the age of the pan. Reproduction warming pans are extremely common.
patience: Very high.

analysis: A doll carriage dated circa 1876 clears the antique line by a wide margin and 'finest quality' plus a specific date suggests the house has something to go on. Period children's carriages with original upholstery and intact wheels are genuinely scarce because they were used to destruction.
problems: Condition is everything and restoration is rampant -- replaced fabric, re-spoked wheels and repaint are all common and all substantially reduce value. The $600-800 estimate assumes original condition.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: Keith, Prowse & Co. was a well-known London music house and a Victorian flutina is a genuinely antique instrument with an attractive case. Six photographs suggests the house thinks the condition supports the $700-900 estimate.
problems: Free-reed instruments of this age almost never play -- bellows leather perishes, reeds corrode and valves curl. Price it as an object rather than an instrument unless you have confirmed it sounds. Restoration costs more than the instrument is worth.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: Three mid-20th-century miniature views of Switzerland -- catalogued as mid-century, so no antique claim, no Maine connection, no named maker, and no precious metal. It fits nothing in the brief.
problems: Tourist paintings in quantity are a category that does not appreciate.
patience: Irrelevant.

analysis: Three consecutive Picasso lots at $300-400 each is the suspiciously cheap big name the brief warns about, and the warning applies exactly. Nothing genuinely by Picasso lands at $300 hammer. These will be later lithographic reproductions, Verve or Cahiers d'Art plates, or unsigned exhibition-poster material.
problems: The catalogue gives the artist's name and dates and nothing else -- no medium, no edition, no date. That silence is the whole story. Note that lot 1150 in the same sale is explicitly catalogued 'after Pablo Picasso', which tells you how the house describes this material when it commits.
patience: Irrelevant -- continuously available.

analysis: The catalogue does the work for you here: after Wheatley, and 1920s re-issues. Both phrases are disqualifying. 'After' means copy, and a 1920s reissue of an 18th-century image is a 1920s object.
problems: Twenty-two sheets at $300-400 sounds like value per sheet, which is how quantity lots are made to look cheap. Cries of London reissues are among the most common decorative prints in existence.
patience: Irrelevant.

analysis: A Deco ivory blotter and monogrammed paperweight is a modest desk set, post-dating the antique line, with a monogram that limits its appeal further. More importantly it carries the ivory complication for no compensating quality.
problems: Elephant ivory is subject to federal Endangered Species Act restrictions on interstate commerce and to documentation requirements that the auction house is unlikely to supply. Buying it in-state at a Maine sale is the simplest case, but it constrains anything you might ever do with it afterwards. Not worth the friction on a $200 desk accessory.
patience: Irrelevant.
